selected_assets.alt_text: Eratosthenes measurement diagram showing Syene, Alexandria, Sun rays, verticals, and a 7.1 degree angle.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: A small set of observations and measurements can support a model-based inference when the geometry and evidence are connected explicitly.
selected_assets.why_here: Opens the unit with a concrete example of observation, inference, evidence, and a meaning-bearing physical relationship.

selected_assets.alt_text: A tablecloth is pulled quickly from beneath dishes on a table.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: The dishes tend to maintain their current state of motion; inertia describes that property and is not an extra force.
selected_assets.why_here: Provides the concrete phenomenon before formalizing Newton’s First Law and the inertia misconception.

selected_assets.alt_text: A table pushes up on a book and a spring pushes up on a hand; downward and upward force arrows are shown.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: A supported object can have multiple nonzero forces that balance; “forces act” and “net force is zero” are different statements.
selected_assets.why_here: Makes support force, weight, and zero-net-force reasoning visible before force-model practice.

selected_assets.alt_text: Perpendicular vectors form a rectangle whose diagonal is the resultant.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: Arrow direction and length carry physical information, and the resultant is a vector rather than an unsigned total.
selected_assets.why_here: Establishes vector meaning and prepares students to read resultant direction and relative size from diagrams.

selected_assets.alt_text: A 30-N vector and a 40-N vector produce a 50-N resultant.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: The resultant depends on both force magnitudes and directions; vector structure determines how forces combine.
selected_assets.why_here: Supports the transition from qualitative vector meaning to net-force/resultant reasoning and calculation.

selected_assets.alt_text: Force vectors on a sign-painting scaffold show upward forces balancing downward forces.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: Individual forces can be nonzero while their vector sum is zero; equilibrium is a net-force condition, not the absence of forces.
selected_assets.why_here: Provides a single durable reference model for static equilibrium, force balance, and missing-force reasoning.

selected_assets.alt_text: Box moving at constant speed with a push and friction in a constant-speed force diagram.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: Constant straight-line motion can coexist with nonzero balanced forces; constant velocity does not mean “no forces.”
selected_assets.why_here: Makes dynamic equilibrium concrete immediately before the representation-consistency pair.

selected_assets.alt_text: Flawed force diagram for a cart rolling at constant speed.
selected_assets.what_students_should_notice: A force model must match the chosen object and the observed motion; a plausible-looking diagram can still contradict the evidence.
selected_assets.why_here: Anchors the culminating model-critique story and prepares students to revise a flawed representation using physics vocabulary.

summary_targets: Classify static and dynamic equilibrium from motion evidence.
Explain how nonzero forces can balance on an object at rest.
Use ΣF=0 to reason about missing balancing forces.
Connect constant straight-line velocity—not merely constant speed—to dynamic equilibrium.
common_mistakes: Assuming constant speed always means equilibrium even when direction changes.
Assuming forces disappear when an object is in equilibrium.

sections.title: Modeling Forces in the Real World
sections.learning_target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

i_cans.text: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

wtc.bank_evidence_job: navigate a multipart model-critique task: identify the system, inspect a shared flawed model/evidence set, plan a revision, and defend the revised motion explanation
wtc.placement: Early: after Learning Target / exact I-can overview and vocabulary terms-only preview, before full teaching story.
wtc.purpose_in_notes_flow: Preview the section’s eventual multipart reasoning without solving it; students annotate what looks familiar and what may matter later.
wtc.surrounding_teacher_framing_for_4B: Keep the WTC prompt unchanged. Frame it as noticing/navigation practice, not a solved example; return to its ideas only through later teaching and the section summary.

story_beats.concept_title: Choose the object before drawing forces
story_beats.reading_goal: A force model begins by defining the object/system being modeled.
essential_ideas: A force model begins by defining the object/system being modeled.
Include only forces acting on that chosen object and label interactions clearly.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Drawing forces that act on another object instead of the chosen system.
Omitting support force or weight in familiar situations.

processing_anchor.reason: The canonical pair directly processes the concept/representation just developed, so no extra Stop & Discuss is inserted at this beat.

story_beats.concept_title: Use the diagram to decide balanced or unbalanced
story_beats.reading_goal: Compare vector directions and relative sizes to decide whether net force is zero.
essential_ideas: Compare vector directions and relative sizes to decide whether net force is zero.
Balanced/unbalanced is a statement about the vector sum, not the number of arrows.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Drawing forces that act on another object instead of the chosen system.
Omitting support force or weight in familiar situations.

processing_anchor.reason: The canonical pair directly processes the concept/representation just developed, so no extra Stop & Discuss is inserted at this beat.

story_beats.concept_title: Net force predicts motion change
story_beats.reading_goal: A nonzero net force identifies the direction of acceleration/motion change without requiring a claim that motion points the same way.
essential_ideas: A nonzero net force identifies the direction of acceleration/motion change without requiring a claim that motion points the same way.
Explanations should cite the force model and motion evidence.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Drawing forces that act on another object instead of the chosen system.
Omitting support force or weight in familiar situations.

processing_anchor.reason: The canonical pair directly processes the concept/representation just developed, so no extra Stop & Discuss is inserted at this beat.

story_beats.concept_title: Critique a model against the evidence
story_beats.reading_goal: A polished-looking force diagram can be wrong if it uses the wrong system, omits an interaction, or conflicts with observed motion.
essential_ideas: A polished-looking force diagram can be wrong if it uses the wrong system, omits an interaction, or conflicts with observed motion.
Revision should name what is wrong, repair the representation, and explain why the revised model is more consistent with the evidence.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Drawing forces that act on another object instead of the chosen system.
Omitting support force or weight in familiar situations.
